algorithmic-interviews-complexity-analys.core: Complexity analysis predicts how time and memory grow with input size. Simplify to the dominant term, know the common classes, specify best/average/worst case, count space including the call stack, use recursion trees for recursive code, and amortise costs over sequences.

first_principles.problem: Solutions that work on tiny examples collapse at production scale.
truths: Growth rate dominates at large n.

analogy.title: A vehicle's fuel economy chart
analogy.story: It tells you how far you can go before you run out, regardless of today's traffic.
analogy.breaks: Fuel economy is linear; algorithm costs can be quadratic or exponential.

example.title: Analysing a two-sum solution
flow: Brute force: O(n²) time, O(1) space
Hash map: O(n) time, O(n) space

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: State both time and space, then justify the trade-off.

check.q: Give the time and space of a hash-map two-sum.
check.a: O(n) time and O(n) space.

algorithmic-interviews-core-data-structu.core: Core data structures each make some operations cheap: arrays for indexed access, dynamic arrays for growable sequences, linked lists for O(1) splicing, stacks for LIFO, queues for FIFO and hash maps for O(1) lookup. Choosing well starts from the operations a problem needs.

first_principles.problem: The wrong structure silently turns an O(n) solution into O(n²).
truths: Each structure has a cost profile.

analogy.title: A workshop of specialised tools
analogy.story: The right tool makes the job trivial; the wrong one makes it painful.
analogy.breaks: Tools don't have amortised costs; dynamic arrays and hash maps do.

example.title: First non-repeating character
example.outcome: efficient solutions from the right tools.

check.q: Which structure gives O(1) average membership checks?
check.a: A hash set (hash map).

algorithmic-interviews-trees-graphs.core: Trees and graphs model hierarchies and networks. Binary search generalises to monotonic predicates, sorting is divide and conquer, DP caches overlapping subproblems, trees are solved by choosing a traversal, and graphs by BFS or DFS with a visited set.

first_principles.problem: Many interview problems look different but share a few structural patterns.
truths: Hierarchies are trees; relationships are graphs.
Divide and conquer gives log factors.

analogy.title: Navigating family trees and road maps
analogy.story: Same skills: follow branches, avoid revisiting and remember what you've worked out.
analogy.breaks: Real maps have distances; weighted graphs need Dijkstra, not plain BFS.

example.title: Course schedule
flow: DFS with colours detects a cycle

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Model first, then pick the traversal.

check.q: Which traversal gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
check.a: Breadth-first search.

algorithmic-interviews-essential-algorit.core: A few algorithmic recipes solve most problems: binary search halves sorted or monotonic spaces, merge and quick sort divide and conquer, recursion reduces problems to smaller selves, and dynamic programming caches overlapping subproblems top-down or bottom-up.

first_principles.problem: Without core recipes, every problem feels new.
truths: Halving and caching are powerful levers.

analogy.title: Mother sauces in French cooking
analogy.story: Master five base sauces and you can make hundreds of dishes.
analogy.breaks: Sauces forgive small errors; off-by-one bugs don't.

example.title: Longest increasing subsequence
flow: DP O(n²): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for a[j] < a[i]
Binary search O(n log n) on tails array

check.q: Name the two DP styles.
check.a: Top-down memoisation and bottom-up tabulation.

algorithmic-interviews-common-patterns.core: Interview problems cluster into patterns with recognisable cues: sliding window for contiguous ranges, two pointers for sorted pairs, greedy when local choices are provably safe, backtracking for exhaustive choices and topological sort for dependencies. Recognising the pattern is most of the solution.

first_principles.problem: Treating every problem as new wastes interview time.

analogy.title: Chess openings
analogy.story: Strong players recognise positions and know the standard plans.
analogy.breaks: Chess opponents adapt; interview problems may combine patterns, so stay flexible.

example.title: Minimum window substring
flow: Cue: smallest contiguous substring containing all chars
Expand until valid, shrink to minimise

check.q: Which pattern fits 'order tasks with dependencies'?
check.a: Topological sort.

algorithmic-interviews-sre-problems.core: SRE coding challenges are production problems in miniature: parse messy logs, stream files larger than memory, merge time intervals, and implement rate limiters and load-balancing algorithms. Success means correctness, bounded resources and operational reasoning.

first_principles.problem: Reliability engineering needs code that survives real data and real scale.
truths: Real data is messy and large.

analogy.title: A firefighter's practical drills
analogy.story: Real hoses, real smoke, real time pressure.
analogy.breaks: Drills end; production systems run forever, so think about long-term behaviour.

example.title: Computing an SLO from logs
flow: Count good vs total per window
Merge outage intervals for the report

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Small building blocks combine into real tools.

check.q: Name two rate-limiting algorithms.
check.a: Token bucket and sliding window (also fixed window and leaky bucket).

algorithmic-interviews-system-design.core: System design interviews test structured trade-off thinking: clarify requirements, estimate with powers of 2 and latency numbers, sketch a high-level design, then deep dive into scaling and failures using a standard toolkit (caches, replicas, shards, queues, load balancers).

first_principles.problem: Open-ended design questions overwhelm candidates without a method.
truths: Structure makes the most of limited time.

analogy.title: An architect's design review
analogy.story: Brief, sizing, concept sketch, then engineering details and costs.
analogy.breaks: Real projects iterate for months; interviews compress it into an hour.

example.title: Design a news feed
flow: Design: post service, fan-out workers, feed cache
Deep dive: celebrity fan-out on read vs write

check.q: Why estimate scale in a design interview?
check.a: Orders of magnitude determine which components and scaling techniques are actually needed.

staff-plus-system-design.core: Staff+ system design shifts from 'how to build it' to 'why, and what's the best bet for the organisation': handling ambiguity, quantifying NFRs and SLOs, choosing buy vs build, eliminating single points of failure and communicating decisions through design documents.

first_principles.problem: Senior engineers can design systems; Staff+ engineers must choose the right systems and align people around them.
truths: Decisions must be communicated and recorded.

analogy.title: A chief architect for a city district
analogy.story: Balancing budgets, residents' needs and future growth, then documenting the plan for everyone.
analogy.breaks: City plans last decades; software strategies need revisiting yearly.

example.title: Platform migration proposal
flow: Why: on-call load from legacy queue

check.q: Name three Staff+ design concerns beyond pure architecture.
check.a: Business alignment, buy vs build/TCO and communicating decisions via RFCs (also SLOs and team constraints).

behavioral-mastery.core: Behavioural mastery is about showing, through concrete STAR stories, how you work with people: leading without authority, resolving conflict with SBI, disagreeing and committing, and growing others through mentoring and sponsorship.

first_principles.problem: Technical skill alone stops predicting impact at senior levels.

analogy.title: A team captain
analogy.story: Skill earns the armband; leadership keeps the team winning.
analogy.breaks: Captains are appointed; engineers earn influence informally.

example.title: Preparing for a loop
flow: Map each to themes (conflict, failure, leadership)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every question has a strong, specific story.

check.q: What does STAR stand for?
check.a: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

offer-negotiation-psychology.core: Offer negotiation is a learnable professional skill: treat yourself as a business, build a strong BATNA, manage anchoring, value public RSUs as cash and pre-IPO equity as probabilistic, account for refreshers and forfeited equity, and negotiate collaboratively with specific asks.

first_principles.problem: Engineers leave large amounts of compounding compensation on the table through discomfort or misunderstanding.

analogy.title: A professional deal negotiation
analogy.story: Prepared, calm, data-backed, and aiming for an agreement both sides like.
analogy.breaks: Business deals involve lawyers; yours involves a recruiter who is also an ally.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Preparation does most of the work.

check.q: What is a BATNA?
check.a: Your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you'll do if this deal falls through.

live-debugging-interviews.core: Live debugging interviews reward a detective's method: observe before acting, sweep vitals in 60 seconds, then use strace (syscalls), tcpdump (packets) and /proc (kernel state) to test hypotheses, all while narrating your reasoning.

first_principles.problem: Broken systems under time pressure tempt random fixes.

analogy.title: An emergency room doctor
analogy.story: Triage vitals, run targeted tests, treat, and confirm recovery, explaining each step to the team.
analogy.breaks: Patients can describe symptoms; systems need you to ask the right tools.

example.title: App times out connecting to its DB
flow: Security group missing rule → fix → verify

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Move down the stack with evidence.

check.q: Which tool shows whether packets actually reach a host?
check.a: tcpdump.

organizational-problem-solving.core: Organisational problem solving applies engineering rigour to people systems: diagnose broken teams before acting, address toxic behaviour directly, structure crises with clear roles, restore motivation through autonomy, mastery and purpose, and learn from failure blamelessly.

first_principles.problem: Many engineering failures are organisational, and technical fixes don't touch them.

analogy.title: Debugging a distributed system made of people
analogy.story: Observability (1:1s), root cause analysis and careful changes, then measure again.
analogy.breaks: People react to being observed and changed, which code doesn't.

example.title: An interview question
flow: Cause: hidden dependencies on another team

check.q: What's the first step for an underperforming team?
check.a: Diagnose the root cause by listening to people and examining data.

concurrency-coding.core: Concurrency coding means keeping shared state correct under unpredictable interleavings. Locks give safety at a throughput cost; reader-writer locks favour read-heavy data; deadlocks arise from the four Coffman conditions and are prevented by lock ordering; atomics and CAS enable lock-free updates.

first_principles.problem: Concurrent code that works in tests fails randomly in production.

analogy.title: Traffic engineering
analogy.story: Signals for safety, multiple lanes for throughput and rules that prevent gridlock.
analogy.breaks: Traffic jams are visible; concurrency bugs hide until rare timings occur.

example.title: Thread-safe bounded queue
flow: Producers wait when full; consumers when empty

check.q: Why wait on a condition inside a while loop?
check.a: Spurious wakeups and competing threads mean the condition may not hold when you wake.

bar-raiser-perspective.core: Big-tech hiring adds structures to protect standards: independent bar raisers with veto power, rubric-based behavioural scoring, red flags like NIH syndrome, and hiring committees that decide from written packets. Understanding these lets you present clear, rubric-aligned, well-documented signal.

first_principles.problem: Candidates optimise for the interviewer in the room but are judged by processes beyond it.

analogy.title: Submitting a paper to peer review
analogy.story: Reviewers you never meet judge it against criteria, from what's on the page.
analogy.breaks: Papers can be revised; interviews are one-shot, so preparation matters.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Prepare for the process, not just the questions.

check.q: What power does a bar raiser typically have?
check.a: Veto power over the hire.

personal-branding.core: Personal branding makes your skills discoverable and credible: a keyword-optimised LinkedIn, writing and talks as proof of expertise, a curated GitHub portfolio and a network built by giving value. Together they turn opportunities from something you chase into something that finds you.

first_principles.problem: Skilled engineers are invisible beyond their immediate team.

analogy.title: A reputation in a trade guild
analogy.story: Craftspeople known for quality work get commissions by word of mouth.
analogy.breaks: Guilds were local; online reputation spreads globally.

check.q: Name three channels for building an engineering brand.
check.a: LinkedIn, a blog or writing, and public speaking (also GitHub and communities).

mock-interview-platforms.core: Mock interviews are flight simulators for hiring: realistic practice under observation, across peer and expert platforms. Switching to the interviewer's seat builds perspective, and asking pointed questions turns polite feedback into targeted improvement.

first_principles.problem: Solo practice doesn't prepare you for the pressure and communication demands of real interviews.

analogy.title: Dress rehearsals for a play
analogy.story: Full costume, lights and audience reveal what script readings never will.
analogy.breaks: Plays repeat the same script; interviews change questions, so practise skills, not lines.

example.title: A month of mocks
flow: Real loop: offer at target level

check.q: Why do mock interviews outperform solo practice?
check.a: They train communication and composure under observation and provide outside feedback.

consulting-and-advisory.core: Consulting and advisory work turns expertise into a business: understand the real economics against employment, price for outcomes, protect engagements with a clear SOW, structure advisory roles properly and win clients through niche positioning and referrals.

first_principles.problem: Engineers move into consulting without the business skills it requires.

analogy.title: Opening a specialist workshop
analogy.story: Craft skill is necessary, but pricing, contracts and reputation decide survival.
analogy.breaks: Workshops sell physical goods; consultants sell judgement, which is harder to price.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Run it like a business from day one.

check.q: What document defines a consulting engagement's scope?
check.a: The Statement of Work (SOW).

bar-raiser-psychology.core: Bar-raiser psychology: the veto-holder is often hidden and probes deeply, lukewarm loops fail for lack of conviction, and skeptics are won by ownership, depth and composure. Prepare every round as if it's the decisive one and give interviewers memorable evidence.

first_principles.problem: Candidates misread the dynamics of high-bar hiring decisions.
truths: Any interviewer may hold the veto.

analogy.title: Auditioning for an orchestra
analogy.story: Every judge matters, a memorable performance wins, and handling a tough passage calmly impresses.
analogy.breaks: Auditions are often blind; interviews judge you as a person too.

example.title: Loop strategy
flow: Map best stories to each round
End each round with a crisp summary

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Plan for the debrief, not just the interview.

check.q: What is the 'conviction trap'?
check.a: Being adequate everywhere without giving any interviewer strong reasons to champion you.

equity-liquidity-taxes.core: Startup equity is valuable but illiquid, and taxes can arrive before cash. Understand paper vs liquid value, liquidity routes (tenders, secondaries), the tax differences between ISOs, NSOs and RSUs, the AMT trap and the 90-day exercise window.

first_principles.problem: Engineers make costly, irreversible equity decisions without understanding liquidity or tax.
truths: Private shares can't easily be sold.
Tax rules depend on equity type and timing.

analogy.title: Owning shares in a family business
analogy.story: Valuable, but selling needs approval, and inheritance tax can come due anyway.
analogy.breaks: Family businesses rarely go public; startups aim to, which changes liquidity entirely.

example.title: An exercise strategy
flow: Year 1: early exercise + 83(b) at tiny spread
Year 3: IPO, sell gradually for LTCG

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Plan ahead of events, not after.

check.q: What is the main AMT risk with ISOs?
check.a: Owing tax on the exercise spread even though the shares can't be sold and may lose value.

burnout-recovery.core: Burnout is a physiological and organisational problem: crunch degrades cognition and quality, rest must be active to restore, boundaries protect recovery, and returning safely requires a practised ability to say no and make trade-offs visible.

first_principles.problem: Engineering culture normalises overwork until people break.
truths: Chronic stress harms performance and health.

analogy.title: Athlete training cycles
analogy.story: Hard training, then planned recovery, or performance collapses through overtraining.
analogy.breaks: Athletes have coaches enforcing rest; engineers must often enforce it themselves.

example.title: A recovery plan
flow: Return with explicit priorities and boundaries

check.q: Why is crunch counterproductive beyond short bursts?
check.a: Fatigue reduces cognitive performance and increases errors, so output per hour and quality drop.

algorithmic-interviews-career-strategy.core: Career strategy treats you as a product: package skills in an impact-focused résumé, demonstrate them with STAR stories, price them by understanding total compensation, and track wins in a brag document that feeds promotion packets mapped to the next level's rubric.

first_principles.problem: Good engineers under-earn and under-advance because they don't manage their careers deliberately.

analogy.title: Running your career like a startup
analogy.story: Clear product, strong pitch, smart pricing and metrics to show growth.
analogy.breaks: Startups pivot freely; careers have reputations that carry over.

example.title: A yearly career cycle
flow: Promo packet when evidence is complete

check.q: How does a brag document support promotions?
check.a: It provides dated, specific evidence that can be mapped to the next level's rubric.
